content.thinking:
Looking at the cross-validation results, I notice something concerning: held-out crowd agreement peaks at wd=1 while true gold dev accuracy actually peaks at wd=3, and the ranking of weight decay values differs between the two metrics. This suggests that validating against noisy crowd labels can be misleading compared to validating against real gold-standard accuracy.

I'm also seeing that with low weight decay, the model overfits to the crowd labels (near-perfect train fit) but this hurts gold accuracy much more severely than it hurts crowd agreement — under simple symmetric label noise, these two metrics should rank models the same way linearly, so the fact that they diverge tells me the crowd errors aren't random noise independent of the input; they're at least partly predictable from the features themselves.

The class-mean decomposition isn't conclusive given noisy small-norm means. I'm now considering whether the crowd noise could be instance-dependent, like coming from a weaker systematic classifier whose errors correlate with x — in that case even perfect modeling of p(crowd|x) would cap achievable gold accuracy, and regularization could help simply by smoothing over those noisy regions.

Testing this against symmetric noise assumptions, though: under x-independent noise, agreement should scale affinely with gold accuracy, but plugging in the actual numbers (0.68, 0.517) and (0.553, 0.502) gives a slope of about 0.12, far below the ~0.7 expected — so the symmetric noise model doesn't fit well either.

I'm also noting that dev and the held-out sample should share the same distribution and crowd process, yet dev's gold class distribution diverges from the crowd's (0.487 vs 0.378 for class 4), suggesting noise is pulling probability mass away from the majority class rather than being uniform across x.

I don't have crowd labels for dev rows or gold labels for sample rows, so I'm trying to figure out how to estimate p(crowd|x) on dev indirectly — comparing my low-weight-decay ensemble (0.622 agreement with gold) versus high-weight-decay (0.699) on the rows where they disagree to see which pattern looks more like genuine crowd noise near decision boundaries.

One explanation is simple overfitting from too few rows relative to parameters, causing memorization rather than a real noise signal, but without gold labels on the sample I can't directly test this with a synthetic experiment. I'm instead looking at how crowd-agreement and gold-agreement trend together across different weight-decay settings — wd=8 giving 0.460/0.619, wd=3 giving 0.517/0.680 — to see if there's a consistent relationship I can exploit.

Comparing observed crowd-agreement against predictions from a symmetric-noise model with η≈0.3: the heavily regularized models (wd=3, wd=8) fit this model well, but the under-regularized ones (wd=1, wd=0.3) show excess agreement the symmetric model can't explain. That points to instance-dependent noise rather than pure symmetric noise — the crowd errors aren't random but have some predictable, x-dependent structure, suggesting the crowd labels were generated with a systematic error component rather than uniform random flipping.

But if gold confidence is lower (Bayes accuracy near 0.8), there are regions where the crowd argmax defaults to f(x) instead of the true label, meaning a perfect crowd model caps out below true gold accuracy, while heavy regularization might smooth over high-frequency noise patterns. Since I can't determine the true noise structure, I'm weighing whether to just stick with a simple, strongly regularized fixed config and trust the learning curve, though the right weight-decay direction at 80000 rows remains unclear given how x-dependent the noise seems to be.

The grid results show the optimal weight decay drifting down as n grows — 8 at n=500, down to 3 around n=2000-4000, with wd=3 clearly winning at n=4000 (0.695 vs 0.662 at wd=5 and 0.634 at wd=1), while at n=2000 the curve is flatter between wd=3 and wd=5. Extrapolating, the optimum might land near 1-1.5 by n=80000, so sticking with wd=3 could cost a few points of accuracy versus the true optimum, though overall accuracy should still be solid — I'm just not fully certain.

I should figure out the ceiling: training a model on the 1000 gold-labeled dev rows with cross-validation would tell me what supervised accuracy looks like with clean labels, giving a useful comparison against the 0.695 achieved with 4000 crowd-labeled rows. On the production side, I'm wary that raw crowd agreement is a biased validation signal since it favors under-regularized models, so I'm considering alternatives like consensus-based label cleaning to get a less biased signal for model selection.

Co-teaching seems promising — training two models and filtering out training examples where labels disagree with confident model consensus, a standard noisy-label technique that handles instance-dependent noise reasonably well. Another option is self-training: first fit a heavily regularized model, use it to relabel points where it's confident but disagrees with the crowd, then retrain a less-regularized model on the corrected labels and check if that helps on dev. I'm also weighing k-NN label smoothing in feature space — with 80,000 rows, averaging crowd labels over neighbors could estimate local label distributions well, though I realize this is essentially what the model is already doing implicitly.

Given the time constraints, I should test ideas on the smaller sample (n≈4000 and subsamples), since improvements that hold from n=1000 to 4000 will likely generalize to the full 80,000. My plan is to first run the ceiling diagnostic — training on gold labels with cross-validation against dev — then quickly try label-correction and co-teaching. I considered a synthetic control using dev gold labels with injected symmetric noise to test whether "crowd agreement is misleading" holds, but the sample is too small for that to be meaningful, so I'll skip it and instead explore whether crowd errors follow a consistent, exploitable pattern, like systematic confusion between certain label pairs.

Checking where the low-weight-decay model gets things wrong on dev, I don't see a single consistent "confuser" class — for gold class 4, errors spread across many different predicted classes rather than concentrating on one. So that structural hypothesis doesn't hold up. I'll move on to examining the ceiling diagnostic results now.

content.text: Re-running the 5-fold study showed a critical fact: held-out crowd agreement does not track gold accuracy (under-regularised models score well on crowd labels but poorly on gold), so the noise is partly predictable from the features and a noisy validation split cannot be trusted for model selection. I'll now measure the achievable ceiling with gold-supervised CV on dev and test label-cleaning strategies that are robust to this kind of noise.

        P=tn.train_one(Xds[tr],yd[tr],200,cfg,wd,seed=f); g.append((tn.predict_proba(P,Xds[va]).argmax(1)==yd[va]).mean())
        idx=rng.choice(4000,800,replace=False); P=tn.train_one(Xs[idx],y[idx],200,cfg,wd,seed=f); c.append((tn.predict_proba(P,Xds[va]).argmax(1)==yd[va]).mean())
    print('800 rows, wd %-3g: gold-trained acc %.3f   crowd-trained acc %.3f'%(wd,np.mean(g),np.mean(c)),flush=True)
# LDA on gold 800 rows
def lda_fit(A,t):
    means=np.array([A[t==c].mean(0) if (t==c).sum()>1 else A.mean(0) for c in range(K)]); pri=(np.bincount(t,minlength=K)+1)/(len(t)+K)
    R=A-means[t]; S=R.T@R/len(A)+0.05*np.eye(A.shape[1]); Si=np.linalg.inv(S)
    return lambda Q: np.array([-0.5*np.einsum('ij,jk,ik->i',Q-m,Si,Q-m)+np.log(p) for m,p in zip(means,pri)]).T
g=[]
for f in range(5):
    va=folds[f]; tr=np.concatenate([folds[k] for k in range(5) if k!=f]); g.append((lda_fit(Xds[tr],yd[tr])(Xds[va]).argmax(1)==yd[va]).mean())
print('LDA gold-trained 800 rows acc %.3f'%np.mean(g))
EOF

Interesting: gold labels with 800 rows give MLP ~0.62 and LDA 0.649, while crowd-trained on 4000 rows reaches 0.695, so the problem seems genuinely hard with a lot of class overlap and an unknown but steep learning curve. Gold labels don't seem to give dramatically higher accuracy at equal sample size compared to crowd labels.

So noise seems to cost roughly 4-5% at this scale, equivalent to needing about twice the data—volume looks like the dominant factor, and since 80000 rows is 20x more, that's reassuring for the larger regime, though I still need to figure out the actual magnitude of improvement and whether hyperparameters stay reasonable. I'm considering how to gather evidence for the 80000-row scale, maybe by building a generative simulator fit on the combined crowd and gold data, though the x-dependent noise mechanism is hard to replicate faithfully. Thinking about it from the data-generation angle instead: this is likely a synthetic challenge task, so X is probably drawn from a Gaussian mixture per class with the gold label as the true class, and the crowd noise might follow an ambiguity-based mechanism where mislabeling swaps in the second-most-likely class under the true posterior.

I'm now considering a fixed confusion matrix mechanism instead, where under class-dependent noise, the crowd argmax can diverge systematically from gold when the matrix is asymmetric—checking whether the crowd class marginals from the dev set match what a symmetric noise model with η≈0.29 would predict, and the numbers are lining up well across several classes so far.

But the noise could still be instance-dependent in which instances get flipped, even if the flip target is uniform random—like boundary examples being more prone to error. This kind of noise still preserves the argmax of the true label distribution since the uniform component doesn't shift which class is most likely, so a perfect model would still predict gold labels. That leaves me puzzled about why the low-weight-decay model shows excess agreement with the crowd, since matching crowd labels on held-out data is maximized by whatever policy best predicts the noisy label distribution itself.

Excess agreement beyond that theoretical relationship could only happen if predictions correlate with actual noise realizations—but held-out rows should have independent noise draws unless the held-out set isn't truly independent from training. That "sample self nearest min 0.0" result suggests there might be exact duplicate rows in the dataset. If some x values repeat with correlated crowd labels, a low-regularization model could memorize the training instance and reproduce that same label when it sees the duplicate at eval time, creating spurious agreement. I want to check how many duplicate rows exist and whether they share crowd labels.

This would explain the pattern entirely: crowd agreement on held-out data reflects memorization leakage through duplicates, while the gold-labeled dev set (with no overlap, nearest squared distance 22) shows no such effect. This also suggests the corpus might contain repeated annotations—the same item labeled multiple times by different crowd workers. If so, the real opportunity at scale is huge: with 80,000 rows, aggregating labels per unique item via majority vote or soft labeling could dramatically denoise the signal, especially since a 5% sample would rarely surface these duplicates while the full corpus would contain them all. Deduping and aggregating could be a major lever here.

Gold-supervised training only beats crowd training by about 4-5 points at equal size, so data volume seems to be the main driver. I'll now check an anomaly—exact duplicate feature rows in the sample—since this could inflate crowd agreement for memorizing models and matters significantly at full corpus scale.
